segments.text: Welcome to the daily Robotics news digest for September 2nd, 2026.
Today we cover breakthroughs in safety assurance, new mobile manipulators, and exciting humanoid challenges.
From The Robot Report, "The Missing Layer in Robot Safety Assurance"

details how robot safety assurance must now account for attacks that manipulate a machine's perception, decisions, and actions, with research indicating that manipulating what a robot sees, hears, or interprets can redirect its behavior without direct control, affecting the entire system.

The report outlines that these attacks can occur across three layers: corrupting intelligence at the source, exploiting system vulnerabilities, and manipulating perception and reasoning at runtime, necessitating the integration of cybersecurity into functional safety to ensure safety throughout the robot's lifecycle.
Safety assurance must now extend beyond functional failure to encompass deliberate manipulation to maintain safe boundaries.
This development requires the AI and technology industry to incorporate robust cybersecurity measures directly into functional safety protocols moving forward.
From Humanoids Daily, Lumos Robotics Unveils MOS 2 Mobile Manipulator Backed by Mitsubishi Factory Deployment.

This report details the introduction of the MOS 2, a wheeled dual-arm mobile manipulator designed for high-mix factory workflows, which demonstrated successful performance in visual inspection and material transport tasks during trials.

Lumos Robotics introduced the MOS 2, a wheeled dual-arm mobile manipulator functioning as an AI Worker with a combined payload capacity of fifty kilograms and a compact footprint measuring zero point five square meters.
Initial testing conducted at a facility of Mitsubishi Electric confirmed the system's operational capability in demanding industrial tasks.
The development of this system is supported by strategic backing from Mitsubishi Electric Smart Manufacturing Technology.
This deployment reflects an industry trend favoring the operational stability and economic viability of wheeled platforms in automated manufacturing environments.
Future developments in mobile robotics will focus on optimizing these wheeled systems for broader industrial application.
From Humanoids Daily, "The No Bot of Theseus"
Challenge: Scott Walter Proposes a Strict Decathlon Benchmark for Humanoids.
This report details a proposed challenge designed to test the generalized physical capability of a single, unmodified humanoid robot across ten track and field events.

The challenge mandates that the robot must operate with strict anthropomorphic constraints, including five-fingered hands and human-proportional sizing, while prohibiting the swapping of any hardware components.

The methodology requires the robot to operate autonomously, log all performance data, and prevent the use of hidden control instructions, further requiring self-dressing and scrutiny of autonomous actions related to performance enhancing instructions.
This unified test is proposed because current humanoids reportedly lack the integrated dexterity and strength necessary for multi-event athletic performance.
The development of such comprehensive benchmarks will inform future advancements in humanoid robotics and embodied artificial intelligence research.
From Planet ROS, ROS Discourse General: Three bugs that changed how our sensor board talks to ROS 2.
This report details three unexpected development issues that necessitated significant changes in the design of a sensor board communicating with ROS 2.
The initial plan to run ROS directly on the chip proved unfeasible due to flash constraints, resulting in the system now utilizing Cyphal with a host-side ROS bridge.
A separate complication arose when a chip failed to fully power off, which required the implementation of a specific reset write operation to manage state retention effectively.
Furthermore, the necessity of accurate timestamps for data fusion was revealed, leading to the implementation of per-sample timestamps alongside sequence numbers.
These findings underscore critical considerations for establishing reliable sensor communication systems.
Developments in this area emphasize the need for robust error handling in embedded systems.
And that's all the circuits for today, September 2nd, 2026.
Hope your algorithms run smoothly!
Keep building amazing things out there.
Until tomorrow, keep those gears turning!
